newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Britain plugs tax loophole on share buybacks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Britain plugs tax loophole on share buybacks.

text.p: The British government on Tuesday plugged a tax loophole giving generous tax benefits to shareholders of companies offering share buyback schemes.

The news came one day before shareholders at the international news and information group Reuters Holdings Plc were due to vote on a 613 million pound ($958 million) share buyback scheme and the company promptly moved to put its plans on hold.

Reponding to a flood of company buybacks granting tax benefits to big shareholders, the government said such shareholders would no longer be able to claim tax credits on share buyacks or special dividend payouts.
Just hours after the government statement, Reuters said it would ask shareholders to adjourn consideration of its share buyback proposals at an extraordinary meeting on Wednesday.

Reuters said it regretted the fact that the British government had proposed amendments to the its tax legislation which would apparently make it more difficult for British firms to return cash to shareholders "in a tax neutral way".

Given the uncertainty created by the government's announcement, Reuters believed it was imprudent to proceed without full details of proposed new government legislation. But it would continue to review the options open to it.
Tax experts said the government announcement appeared directly related to the timing of the Reuters share buyback scheme.
"The timing is no coincidence...it's crystal clear that it's aimed at Reuters special dividend shares," said Roger Muray, tax partner at Ernst & Young.
The government made clear on Tuesday it was scrapping the tax credit scheme to cap a drain on its own finances after a rash of companies had announced buybacks with tax credits.
British finance minister Kenneth Clarke referred to "...the growing loss of tax through schemes involving companies buying their own shares or paying special dividends."

So far this year British firms announced plans to spend up to 2.5 billion pounds ($4 billion) in buying back their own shares, with this total seen rising to four billion pounds by the end of the year.
Share buybacks are most beneficial to tax-exempt shareholders, principally pension funds, who can claim tax credits from the government.

Although Reuters said it would adjourn a decision on its own share buyback scheme, British bank Barclays Plc said the new government ruling would not affect its plans for further repurchases of its own stock.
Reuters shares came under immediate pressure on Tuesday morning following the government's announcement, dropping to a low of 750 pence before settling in mid-afternoon trade at 755, down 22 pence.
Banking and utility groups, also candidates for share buy back schemes, had also seen selling on the London market.

Companies often seek to return excess cash to shareholders if they have no obvious investment alternatives. Tax experts said companies would likely seek new innovative ways of reducing their cash mountains, despite the new government stance.
"The bandwagon may roll on," said Robert Turnbull, a partner at accountancy group KPMG. ($1=.6401 Pound)
